newsitem.title: USA: Grades gain ground against firmer U.S. cash crudes.
newsitem.headline: Grades gain ground against firmer U.S. cash crudes.

text.p: Short covering bolstered U.S. cash crude grade differentials Monday against a firming outright price for benchmark crude in the U.S. Gulf.
August West Texas Intermediate/Cushing virtually tracked the NYMEX screen, as Exchange for Physicals (EFPs) slumped from recent premiums to only a three cents edge against paper.
Benchmark WTI for August was at $19.10-20 a barrel, 25 cents firmer than Friday, while July/August rolls talked late in the session at -30 cents.
Deals were recorded for the roll at July/August -27, -28 and finally -30 cents, traders said.

Market expectations for a lower number of foreign crude deliveries against the July NYMEX contract came true, after the exchange said only 805,000 barrels of foreign supply was delivered. May and June NYMEX contracts attracted 2.73 million and 2.349 million barrels of foreign deliveries.
August EFPs were expected to rest at only a slight premium to the NYMEX screen on news of the absorption of foreign overhang, traders said.

For the grades, July business became quieter heading into pipeline scheduling, but late numbers were stronger than Friday. Midland/WTI July barrels were pegged at 21-18 cents under WTI/Cushing, with Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James at flat to five cents under the marker.
Heavy Louisiana Sweet/Empire talked 40-50 cents cheaper than benchmark, steady from late trackings on Friday.

West Texas Sour/Midland shaved another 10 cents off its differential, selling between 80-90 cents under WTI by session's end. "It just seems like a lot of refiner short covering," said a cash dealer in the Gulf.
Eugene Island was pegged at $1.30 under marker, with July Postings Plus at $1.62-65, a five cents decline from Friday.
August LLS/St. James barrels came in around flat to the market, crude players said.

Outright crude prices continued to trend higher on nervous buying over Iraq tensions, following the weekend move by the U.N. Security Council to warn Baghdad against interfering with arms inspections, or face further sanctions.

Crude values also found support from comments by Iranian oil minister Gholamreza Aghazadeh in Vienna at the semi-annual OPEC meeting. The minister said Iran was not pleased with world oil prices and that OPEC should take measures to curb overproduction by member states.
